headline: GAO Reports $24.3 Billion in Estimated Improper Payments
dek: VA Community Care and Medicare Advantage reported improper-payment estimates of $608 million and $23.7 billion for fiscal 2025; GAO says both lack comprehensive fraud-risk assessments.

sources.title: Program Integrity: Actions Needed to Reduce Improper Payment and Fraud Risks in VA Community Care and Medicare Advantage

lead.creator: Tony Webster
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic, verified by Wikimedia Commons Flickr review.
lead.attribution: Tony Webster / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
lead.caption: A medical exam room. GAO reviewed improper-payment and fraud-risk controls in VA Community Care and Medicare Advantage.
lead.alt: Medical exam room with an examination table, chair, counter and clinical equipment.

charts.caption: Fiscal 2025 improper-payment estimates were $608 million for VA Community Care and $23.7 billion for Medicare Advantage.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 608 million dollars for VA Community Care and 23.7 billion dollars for Medicare Advantage.

charts.caption: GAO made three open recommendations: one to VA and two to CMS.
charts.alt: Graphic lists three open GAO recommendations, one for VA and two for CMS.

paragraphs: The Department of Veterans Affairs and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services reported a combined $24.3 billion in estimated improper payments across two health programs in fiscal 2025, according to the Government Accountability Office.
VA estimated $608 million in improper payments in Community Care, equal to 2.4% of that program's outlays. CMS estimated $23.7 billion in improper payments in Medicare Advantage, or 6.1% of outlays.

An improper payment is not automatically fraud. The category can include overpayments, underpayments, payments made without enough documentation and other errors; GAO assessed payment-error controls and fraud risk as related but distinct issues.

GAO found that both agencies had processes to identify root causes of improper payments. VA also had corrective-action plans that the watchdog said adequately addressed identified causes for the years reviewed.

CMS's Medicare Advantage improper-payment rate had remained steady, GAO said. Its corrective plans were not detailed enough, and the agency lacked a detailed plan to clear a backlog of Risk Adjustment Data Validation audits used to identify and recover improper payments.
Neither agency had completed a comprehensive fraud-risk assessment for the program GAO reviewed. VA had taken some fraud-risk steps, but GAO said they did not cover all key elements of its framework.

GAO issued three recommendations: VA should conduct a comprehensive Community Care fraud-risk assessment, while CMS should create a detailed RADV-audit plan and conduct a Medicare Advantage fraud-risk assessment. All three were open when GAO published the report.

VA concurred with its recommendation. CMS neither agreed nor disagreed with its two recommendations and described actions it believed addressed them; GAO maintained that additional action was warranted.

The accountability measures are whether the agencies complete the assessments, reduce the audit backlog and publish evidence that corrective plans lower error rates. The reported improper-payment estimates do not establish the amount lost to fraud or the amount that can be recovered.
facts: VA Community Care reported $608 million in estimated improper payments for fiscal 2025.
Medicare Advantage reported $23.7 billion in estimated improper payments.
The rates were 2.4% and 6.1% of program outlays, respectively.
Neither program had a comprehensive fraud-risk assessment.
GAO made three recommendations, all open at publication.
uncertainty: Improper-payment estimates are not estimates of fraud losses.
Future recovery and error-rate reductions depend on agency implementation and audit results.
seoDescription: GAO reports $24.3 billion in fiscal 2025 improper-payment estimates across VA Community Care and Medicare Advantage.

headline: USSC Counts 517 National-Defense Cases in Fiscal 2025
dek: The category rose 132% from fiscal 2021, but the Sentencing Commission says a 2025 border designation brought some illegal-entry convictions into the count.
entities: U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas

lead.creator: Ajay Suresh
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International, verified by Wikimedia Commons Flickr review.
lead.attribution: Ajay Suresh / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
lead.caption: The E. Barrett Prettyman United States Courthouse in Washington. The Sentencing Commission counted 517 national-defense cases in fiscal 2025.
lead.alt: Stone federal courthouse with broad steps and columns in Washington, D.C.

charts.caption: National-defense cases numbered 517 of 66,662 federal cases in fiscal 2025, up 132% from fiscal 2021.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 517 national-defense cases, 66,662 total cases and a 132 percent increase since fiscal 2021.

charts.caption: Eighty-five percent received prison sentences, with an average sentence of 21 months across the category.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 85 percent receiving prison and an average sentence of 21 months.

paragraphs: Federal courts sentenced people in 517 cases that the United States Sentencing Commission classified as national-defense offenses in fiscal 2025, 132% more than in fiscal 2021.

Those cases were 0.8% of the 66,662 cases reported to the commission for the year. The category is broader than espionage or terrorism and depends on the sentencing guideline or conduct assigned to each case.

USSC says national-defense cases include offenses under the guideline chapter for national defense and weapons of mass destruction, other guideline cases involving conduct that threatens national defense and cases receiving the terrorism sentencing adjustment.

A 2025 classification change is central to the trend. In April 2025, portions of the U.S.-Mexico border were designated National Defense Areas, and USSC assigned some convictions for illegally entering those locations under 50 U.S.C. § 797 to the national-defense crime type.
The Western District of Texas accounted for 252 cases, followed by the Southern District of Texas with 66, Arizona with 51, Northern Alabama with 49 and Middle Florida with 13.

Eighty-five percent of people sentenced in the category received prison terms. The average sentence was 21 months, but averages varied sharply by offense and by whether the terrorism adjustment applied.

The average was 24 months for unauthorized arms-export cases, 23 months for export-control and terrorism-financing cases, and 111 months for support-to-terrorism cases. People receiving the terrorism adjustment averaged 196 months.

The quick-facts sheet describes sentenced federal cases, not arrests, intelligence investigations or a count of unique threats. It also excludes cases with incomplete sentencing information from some demographic calculations.

The 132% increase therefore needs classification context. A useful follow-up is to separate the 2025 National Defense Area cases from the longer-running national-security categories before interpreting the change as a shift in underlying conduct.
facts: USSC counted 517 national-defense cases in fiscal 2025.
The category rose 132% from fiscal 2021.
The 517 cases were part of 66,662 total cases.
The Western District of Texas accounted for 252 cases.
Eighty-five percent received prison sentences and the average sentence was 21 months.
uncertainty: The category includes some 2025 border-entry convictions because of National Defense Area designations.
Case totals do not measure arrests, investigations or a single homogeneous type of conduct.
seoTitle: USSC counted 517 national-defense cases in fiscal 2025
seoDescription: USSC counted 517 national-defense cases in fiscal 2025, up 132% from 2021, with a border classification change shaping the total.

headline: CBO’s Two Cost Methods Differ by $67.2 Billion for 2027 Federal Credit
dek: The budget method projects $15.3 billion in lifetime savings, while a fair-value method that accounts for market risk projects a $51.9 billion cost.

sources.title: Estimates of the Cost of Federal Credit Programs in 2027

lead.creator: Linuxerist~commonswiki
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported; selected from the file's offered licenses.
lead.caption: A house key. Mortgage guarantees and student loans make up most of the federal credit assistance CBO analyzed for 2027.
lead.alt: Single metal house key resting on a dark surface.

charts.caption: FCRA procedures project $15.3 billion in lifetime savings; fair value projects a $51.9 billion lifetime cost.
charts.alt: Graphic compares 15.3 billion dollars in projected FCRA savings with a 51.9 billion dollar fair-value cost.

charts.caption: CBO analyzed 94 programs projected to provide $1.9 trillion in new loans and guarantees in 2027.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 94 programs and 1.9 trillion dollars in projected federal credit assistance for 2027.

paragraphs: Two methods for measuring the lifetime cost of federal credit programs produce estimates that differ by $67.2 billion for loans and guarantees projected in fiscal 2027, the Congressional Budget Office reported.
Procedures under the Federal Credit Reform Act, the method used in the federal budget, show $15.3 billion in lifetime savings. CBO's fair-value method instead shows a $51.9 billion lifetime cost.
Both estimates use projected cash flows. The fair-value approach adds a market-risk premium, while the FCRA approach discounts projected cash flows using Treasury rates.
CBO analyzed 94 programs projected to provide $1.9 trillion in credit assistance: $216 billion in direct loans and $1.7 trillion in loan guarantees.
Mortgage guarantees and student loans account for 87% of the total. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac alone are projected to provide $1 trillion in new mortgage-backed-security guarantees.
Nearly two-thirds of the gap between the methods comes from Fannie and Freddie guarantees, Housing and Urban Development programs, and Department of Education student loans.

For Fannie and Freddie, FCRA shows $12.5 billion in savings while fair value shows a $3.9 billion cost. HUD credit shifts from $8.7 billion in savings to an $8.1 billion cost, and student-loan costs rise from $3.6 billion to $13.7 billion.

The estimates are projections, not current cash balances. Policy changes, updated data, estimating methods, economic conditions and the characteristics of borrowers can all change projected loan volumes and cash flows.

CBO says fair value is more comprehensive for comparing policy trade-offs because it includes market risk, while FCRA remains the statutory budget measure. The $67.2 billion gap describes a measurement choice, not an accounting error.
facts: CBO analyzed 94 federal credit programs.
Projected 2027 credit assistance totals $1.9 trillion.
FCRA projects $15.3 billion in lifetime savings.
Fair value projects a $51.9 billion lifetime cost.
Mortgage guarantees and student loans account for 87% of projected credit assistance.
uncertainty: The figures are lifetime projections for 2027 lending, not realized cash results.
Economic conditions, policy changes and updated data can change projected costs.
seoTitle: CBO finds $67.2B gap between federal credit cost methods
seoDescription: CBO's FCRA and fair-value methods differ by $67.2 billion on the lifetime cost of federal loans and guarantees projected for 2027.

headline: NSF Project Triad Aims to Link Three Quantum Systems
dek: The initiative would integrate quantum sensing, networking and computing, with a proof-of-concept system planned through the National Quantum Virtual Laboratory.

sources.title: NSF launches Project Triad to advance quantum technology for real-world applications

lead.creator: Oak Ridge National Laboratory
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic, verified by Wikimedia Commons Flickr review.
lead.attribution: Oak Ridge National Laboratory / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
lead.caption: A dilution-refrigerator experiment at Oak Ridge National Laboratory measures spin lifetime and coherence. NSF's Project Triad aims to integrate quantum sensing, networking and computing.
lead.alt: Quantum laboratory equipment surrounding a dilution refrigerator used for spin measurements.

charts.caption: Project Triad is organized around three linked domains: quantum sensing, quantum networking and quantum computing.
charts.alt: Graphic lists quantum sensing, quantum networking and quantum computing as three linked domains.

charts.caption: NSF identifies three program components: NQVL, X-Labs and Quantum+X.
charts.alt: Graphic lists the National Quantum Virtual Laboratory, NSF X-Labs and NSF Quantum plus X.

paragraphs: The U.S. National Science Foundation has launched Project Triad, an initiative intended to integrate quantum sensing, quantum networking and quantum computing into one operational research system.

The three domains perform different jobs. Sensors collect information using quantum effects, networks transfer quantum information, and computers process it. Project Triad's central technical goal is to preserve quantum coherence as information moves through the system.
NSF says the National Quantum Virtual Laboratory will deliver a proof-of-concept integrated system for experimentation and testing. NQVL is in its design phase.

The agency plans to accelerate several NQVL projects from design into implementation by December 2026, subject to funding availability. That date is a program target, not evidence that an integrated system already operates.

NSF X-Labs will organize independent teams of researchers, engineers and entrepreneurs around milestone-based challenges. Interconnects and photonics are among the technologies needed to move quantum information between devices.
A third component, NSF Quantum+X, is meant to work with industry on use cases. NSF is seeking partnerships for initial tracks that could include energy, finance, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals.

NSF describes possible future applications in navigation without satellite access, underground-resource detection and medical imaging. Those examples are prospective and do not establish that Project Triad has demonstrated them.

The project joins government, universities and private industry around a shared test environment. It also draws on existing NSF quantum institutes, engineering centers and research-infrastructure programs rather than replacing them.

The next evidence checkpoints are funded NQVL implementations, interfaces that preserve coherence across sensing, transmission and computation, and independently measured performance on selected use cases. The launch announcement defines a program architecture, not a commercial product.
facts: Project Triad links quantum sensing, networking and computing.
NQVL is assigned to deliver a proof-of-concept integrated system.
NQVL is currently in the design phase.
NSF aims to move several NQVL projects into implementation by December 2026, pending funding.
X-Labs and Quantum+X are the other two program components.
uncertainty: The integrated system has not yet been demonstrated in the launch announcement.
Implementation timing and scope depend on funding, technical milestones and partnerships.
seoTitle: NSF Project Triad links quantum sensors, networks and computers
seoDescription: NSF Project Triad aims to integrate quantum sensing, networking and computing through NQVL, X-Labs and industry partnerships.

headline: NASA Model Tracked Wildfire Brown Carbon Across North America for a Week
dek: The GEOS reconstruction followed smoke from July 14-20 as air quality fell from southern Ontario through parts of the Midwest and Northeast.
entities: NASA Global Modeling and Assimilation Office

sources.title: A Week of Smoky Skies Across North America

lead.creator: Marc A. Hermann / Metropolitan Transportation Authority
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic, verified by Wikimedia Commons Flickr review.
lead.attribution: Marc A. Hermann / MTA, CC BY 2.0
lead.caption: Wildfire smoke shrouded 42nd Street in New York City in June 2023. NASA modeled a separate week of North American wildfire brown carbon in July 2026.
lead.alt: Heavy wildfire smoke turns the sky orange above traffic and pedestrians on a Manhattan street.

charts.caption: NASA's GEOS animation tracked wildfire brown carbon from July 14 through July 20, 2026.
charts.alt: Graphic lists a model window from July 14 through July 20, 2026.

charts.caption: GEOS assimilates satellite, aircraft and ground observations with meteorological data to reconstruct plume behavior.
charts.alt: Graphic lists satellite, aircraft, ground and weather data as inputs to the GEOS model.

paragraphs: NASA's Goddard Earth Observing System model tracked wildfire-produced brown carbon across North America from July 14 through July 20, showing smoke moving through Canada and the United States.
Brown carbon is organic aerosol emitted by fires and a component of wildfire PM2.5. It contributes to the yellow, orange and brown tint of smoke plumes.

The GEOS system assimilates observations from satellites, aircraft and ground instruments with temperature, moisture and wind data. The resulting animation is a model reconstruction, not a camera recording or a single satellite image.
More than 180 fires were active in Ontario on July 14, NASA reported, along with several in northern Minnesota. Winds carried smoke southeast by the following day.

Air quality declined from southern Ontario into the Upper Midwest and Northeast. NASA said Detroit remained in the hazardous range for several consecutive days, while Toronto, Chicago, New York and Washington ranged from unhealthy to hazardous.
Smoke continued to affect the Great Lakes region on July 19 and 20. Storms improved air quality in parts of the East as fires in the Pacific Northwest began degrading conditions there.

The brown-carbon field in the animation represents organic carbon specifically attributed to wildfire smoke. Wildfires also emit black carbon, but black carbon has substantial vehicle and industrial sources that complicate attribution.
A NASA model update in February 2026 separated anthropogenic and biomass-burning organic carbon, allowing the animation to isolate wildfire brown carbon more directly than earlier versions.

The reconstruction explains where modeled smoke moved during one completed week; it is not a current forecast. Current health decisions require local official air-quality readings and advisories rather than the July animation.
facts: The animation covers July 14-20, 2026.
GEOS assimilates satellite, aircraft, ground and meteorological data.
More than 180 fires were active in Ontario on July 14.
Brown carbon is a component of wildfire PM2.5.
A February 2026 model update separated wildfire and human-source organic carbon.
uncertainty: The animation is a model reconstruction and not a direct measurement at every location.
The completed July event does not describe current air quality or forecast future smoke.
seoTitle: NASA tracked wildfire brown carbon across North America
seoDescription: NASA's GEOS model reconstructed wildfire brown carbon across North America from July 14-20, 2026, as air quality deteriorated.

headline: IMF Projects Kazakhstan Growth at 4.6% as Inflation Stays Near 10%
dek: Staff expects the current account to move from a 4.1% deficit in 2025 to a marginal surplus, while warning that inflation remains well above target.

sources.title: IMF Staff Concludes Visit to Kazakhstan

lead.creator: Ken and Nyetta
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic, verified by Wikimedia Commons Flickr review.
lead.attribution: Ken and Nyetta / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
lead.caption: The Astana skyline. IMF staff projects Kazakhstan's economy will grow about 4.6% in 2026 while inflation remains near 10%.
lead.alt: Wide panorama of modern towers and government buildings along the Astana skyline.

charts.caption: IMF staff projects 4.6% growth and inflation around 10% for Kazakhstan in 2026.
charts.alt: Graphic lists projected growth of 4.6 percent and inflation around 10 percent in 2026.

charts.caption: The current account is projected to move from a 4.1% deficit in 2025 to a marginal surplus in 2026.
charts.alt: Graphic shows the current account moving from a 4.1 percent deficit in 2025 to a marginal surplus in 2026.

paragraphs: International Monetary Fund staff projects Kazakhstan's economy will grow about 4.6% in 2026, while inflation remains around 10% and well above the central bank's 5% target.

Real GDP expanded 3.7% in the first five months of 2026, down from 6.5% at the end of 2025. IMF staff attributed the moderation partly to lower oil production after an accident affecting the Caspian Pipeline Consortium.

Services, transport, construction and manufacturing helped offset lower oil output. The 4.6% full-year projection assumes elevated oil prices counter slower household credit growth, stable oil output and fiscal consolidation.
Annual inflation fell from 12.9% in September 2025 to 10.4% in May 2026. The National Bank of Kazakhstan reduced its policy rate by 100 basis points in June after the decline and tighter liquidity.

IMF staff said monetary policy should stay tight until inflation is firmly moving toward target. Utility-price adjustments, external price pressure and faster quasi-fiscal or capital spending could push inflation higher.
The current account is projected to shift from a deficit equal to 4.1% of GDP in 2025 to a marginal surplus in 2026 as stronger exports offset public-investment-related imports.

International reserves cover about 10 months of imports, according to the staff statement. The banking sector was described as well capitalized, liquid and profitable overall, with low, provisioned nonperforming loans.

Risks run in both directions. Strong domestic demand or higher import prices could reignite inflation, while global uncertainty, tighter financial conditions or pipeline disruption could weaken growth; sustained oil prices could strengthen buffers.

These are preliminary staff findings after a June 3-12 visit, not a decision by the IMF Executive Board. The next tests are official growth and inflation data, fiscal execution and whether policy keeps price growth on a durable path toward target.
facts: IMF staff projects 4.6% economic growth in 2026.
Inflation is projected around 10% in 2026.
Real GDP grew 3.7% in the first five months of 2026.
May inflation was 10.4%, down from 12.9% in September 2025.
The current account is projected to move from a 4.1% deficit to a marginal surplus.
uncertainty: The figures are IMF staff projections and do not represent an Executive Board decision.
Oil prices, pipeline conditions, domestic demand and policy execution could change the outlook.
seoTitle: IMF sees Kazakhstan growth at 4.6%, inflation near 10%
seoDescription: IMF staff projects Kazakhstan growth at 4.6% in 2026 and inflation near 10%, with the current account moving toward surplus.
